classification.difficultyReason: Beyond constructing extended altitudes, reinterpret the original three perpendicular relationships as altitudes of triangles containing H. This requires changing each point's role and recognising that the same lines prove concurrency in both acute and obtuse configurations.

children.label: a
children.prompt: On a large sheet of paper, draw an obtuse-angled triangle, then construct its orthocentre. You will need to produce two of the sides to perform this construction.

answer.short: Construction varies. The three altitudes meet outside the obtuse-angled triangle.
answer.worked: Draw an obtuse-angled triangle $ABC$. Extend the two sides meeting at the obtuse angle. Through each opposite vertex, construct a perpendicular to the corresponding extended side. Label their intersection $H$. Construct the perpendicular from the remaining vertex to its opposite side; this also passes through $H$. Thus $H$ is the orthocentre, outside the triangle.

spec.description: Authored example of an obtuse triangle, with two side extensions and all three altitudes meeting outside it. No numerical dimensions are asserted.
spec.mathematics: Triangle ABC is obtuse at C. AH is perpendicular to BC, BH is perpendicular to AC, and CH is perpendicular to AB.
spec.answerVisibility: Example construction appears only in answer editions.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Let $H$ be the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$. Prove that each of the four points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $H$ is the orthocentre of the triangle formed by the other three points. This is true in both cases – when $\triangle ABC$ is acute-angled and when $\triangle ABC$ is obtuse-angled.

answer.short:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are the orthocentres of $\triangle BCH$, $\triangle ACH$ and $\triangle ABH$, respectively; $H$ is the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$.

The same three perpendicular relationships supply the altitudes in each triangle, including when sides must be extended.
answer.worked:
Since $H$ is the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$,
$$AH\perp BC,\qquad BH\perp AC,\qquad CH\perp AB.$$
In $\triangle BCH$, the line $BA$ is perpendicular to $CH$, the line $CA$ is perpendicular to $BH$, and the line $HA$ is perpendicular to $BC$. These three altitudes meet at $A$, so $A$ is its orthocentre.

In $\triangle ACH$, the line $AB$ is perpendicular to $CH$, the line $CB$ is perpendicular to $AH$, and the line $HB$ is perpendicular to $AC$. These three altitudes meet at $B$, so $B$ is its orthocentre.

In $\triangle ABH$, the line $AC$ is perpendicular to $BH$, the line $BC$ is perpendicular to $AH$, and the line $HC$ is perpendicular to $AB$. These three altitudes meet at $C$, so $C$ is its orthocentre.

Together with the given orthocentre $H$ of $\triangle ABC$, this proves all four statements. The argument uses perpendicular lines, so it applies to both acute-angled and obtuse-angled triangles, with sides extended where necessary.
